paper.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the backbone used by metrics for evaluating the quality of generated images. Although generative models have advanced rapidly, some outputs still exhibit unrealistic texture characteristics, and these differences are difficult to measure. Widely used evaluation metrics provide limited insight into texture realism, since they often rely on a backbone trained for another objective, such as image classification or image-text alignment. Such objectives typically encourage invariance to low-level variations that carry texture, so the resulting features primarily encode semantic and global structure. As a result, texture-specific discrepancies may not be explicitly captured. We propose TRIG, a metric directed at the texture realism of generated images. Its backbone is instead the discriminator of a generative adversarial network pre-trained on a texture dataset, which provides a learned prior for the local statistics of natural textures. A plausibility head is fine-tuned to identify local texture degradations, while preserving natural defocus and sensor noise as positive cases. On the features of this backbone, we compute a standard distributional distance between a reference set of real images and a set of generated ones. We apply TRIG to several generative models and observe closer agreement with human realness ratings than baseline metrics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Progress in image generation quality is largely measured by automated metrics. The standard approach compares a set of generated images with a set of real ones in the feature space of a pretrained network, and reports a distance between the two distributions. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al. 2017 ) and the Kernel Inception Distance (KID) ( Bińkowski et al. 2018 ) follow this pattern with features from an image classifier, and CLIP Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) ( Jayasumana et al. 2024 ) follows it with embeddings trained for image-text alignment. A separate line of work ( Sajjadi et al. 2018 ; Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ) reports precision and recall in place of a single distance, in order to distinguish the fidelity of generated samples from their diversity. Although these methods differ in Real DiT ADM StyleGAN-XL Original Images Fourier Spectra Figure 1: Real and generated images with their Fourier spectra. Compared with natural photographs, generated images exhibit characteristic spectral artifacts, particularly in the mid-to-high frequency range, despite appearing visually similar in the image domain. how they compare distributions, they primarily rely on representations learned for particular objectives, and thus influence which discrepancies between real and generated images the resulting metrics are sensitive to. Modern generative models now reproduce scene content and global structure remarkably well, while often differing from photographs in the statistics of local texture. These differences contribute to a perceived lack of realism even when observers cannot point to their source, and they become more evident in the frequency domain (Figure 1 ). Recent work ( Stein et al. 2023 ) has shown that the choice of representation is a major source of disagreement between automated metrics and human judgment, motivating alternatives based on self-supervised representations ( Caron et al. 2021 ; Oquab et al. 2024 ) rather than image classification. Although these representations capture richer visual information, they remain optimized for objectives that encourage invariance to low-level appearance changes, including much of the variation that characterizes texture (see discussion in Section. 3 ). Recent texture-oriented metrics ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) likewise extract statistics from such backbones, which can be limited for assessing texture realism itself. Texture realism, however, is not equivalent to sharpness. Real photographs naturally contain blur, sensor noise, and other imperfections arising from the image formation process: backgrounds fall outside the depth of field ( Levoy and Hanrahan 1996 ) , moving objects produce motion blur ( Levin et al. 2008 ) , and photon-limited imaging introduces visible noise under low illumination ( Foi et al. 2008 ) . Therefore, measuring whether the local texture is consistent with statistics derived from physical image formation remains challenging. Motivated by this perspective, we learn a representation specifically for texture realism instead of adapting one trained for another task. We begin with the discriminator of a generative adversarial network (GANs) ( Goodfellow et al. 2014 ; Liu et al. 2019 ; Lin et al. 2023 ) trained on textures, whose objective is to distinguish real textures from synthesized ones. The early layers are kept frozen to preserve this learned texture prior, while a lightweight prediction head is trained to produce dense spatial features. Training such prediction head uses only real photographs, where synthetic degradations are adaptively applied. The degradations are chosen to produce texture statistics that are unlikely to arise through physical image formation. As such, the resulting representation produces, at each spatial location, a score reflecting consistency with learned natural-texture statistics. For evaluating generative models, these features are pooled within each image and compared across image sets using a distributional distance. We refer to the resulting metric as TRIG. We evaluate TRIG on various generative models and compare it with widely used automatic metrics. We also examine our metric for agreement with two human studies, where in both settings, TRIG exhibits closer agreement with human judgments than the competing metrics. We further analyze the spatial responses of the learned representation, showing that both the image-level score and the texture-realism map identify regions whose texture can differ from that of real photographs. Finally, ablation studies examine the contribution of each component of the proposed method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce TRIG , a distributional metric that evaluates generative models through a representation learned specifically for texture realism. • We propose a spatially supervised texture representation by adapting a texture GAN discriminator and fine-tuning it with localized synthetic degradations. • We apply TRIG to various generative models and find that TRIG better agrees with human judgments of texture realism than widely used metrics, while providing spatial maps that localize inconsistent texture.

sections.heading: Metrics for image generation.
sections.text: Most evaluation metrics compare generated and real images in the feature space of a pretrained network. The Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al. 2016 ) summarizes the predictions of an image classifier, while FID ( Heusel et al. 2017 ) and KID ( Bińkowski et al. 2018 ) compare feature distributions extracted by the same backbone using Fréchet and kernel distances, respectively. CMMD replaces the classification features with representations from a vision-language model. Complementary metrics report precision and recall, or density and coverage, to separately characterize sample fidelity and diversity ( Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ; Naeem et al. 2020 ) . Several studies examine the reliability of these metrics, and most target the Inception representation they rely on rather than the comparison itself. Parmar et al. (2022) show that low-level operations such as aliased resizing and compression alter the extracted features and thus the reported score, and propose corrected preprocessing. Chong and Forsyth (2020) show that the FID estimator is biased in a way that depends on the model being evaluated, and derive a debiased variant. CMMD ( Jayasumana et al. 2024 ) instead changes both components: it replaces Inception with CLIP features and the Fréchet distance with the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). These works patch the backbone, debias the estimator, or substitute a different generic backbone, but none learn a representation tailored to texture; this is the gap our method addresses.

sections.heading: The choice of feature extractor.
sections.text: Recent work argues that the representation largely determines agreement with human perception. ( Stein et al. 2023 ) show that classification features correlate poorly with human judgments and recommend replacing them with self-supervised feature extractors, such as DINOv2-ViT-L/14 ( Oquab et al. 2024 ) . Gram-MMD ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) instead targets texture by computing Gram statistics from intermediate features of a pretrained backbone selected through a search over layers. Despite these differences, all of these methods rely on representations learned for object recognition other than texture assessment. We instead train a representation specifically for texture realism by adapting a texture discriminator and fine-tuning it with supervision designed for this task.

sections.heading: From texture representation to image quality assessment.
sections.text: The statistical description of texture has a long history in image processing, originally developed for texture synthesis. ( Portilla and Simoncelli 2000 ) represent a texture by a compact set of multiscale wavelet statistics and re-synthesize textures that match them. ( Gatys et al. 2015 ) and ( Heitz et al. 2021 ) instead extract features from a pretrained VGG ( Simonyan and Zisserman 2015 ) network, matching either their Gram matrices or, in the case of ( Heitz et al. 2021 ) , their full feature distributions via a sliced Wasserstein distance. In all cases the goal is to find a representation in which two textures that look alike are close, and to synthesize a texture that matches a target under that representation. This suggests a natural extension to evaluation: if similar textures yield similar representations, then the distance between representations can measure texture similarity. Gram-MMD follows this idea by computing MMD over Gram statistics extracted from selected layers of a pretrained backbone. We adopt the same premise, but argue that the representation should be learned for texture realism instead of a second-order statistic of features from a backbone trained for an unrelated semantic task.

sections.heading: Texture Quality in Real Imaging
sections.text: We study the problem of assessing the texture quality of images produced by generative models. By texture quality , we mean the consistency between local texture statistics in images and those in real images. A real image may contain a defocused background, motion blur from a moving subject, or sensor noise in a dimly lit region. These effects can arise naturally during image formation and therefore do not by themselves indicate unrealistic texture. Generated images may instead exhibit local texture discrepancies that are not explained by these natural effects, such as spatially inconsistent loss of high-frequency detail (see Figure. 1 for examples with their Fourier spectra). The question we ask of an image is therefore not how sharp it is, but whether its texture is consistent with the surrounding visual context. These objectives reward invariance to the low-level variation that carries texture, so the resulting features encode mainly semantic and global structure. As shown in Figure. 2 , under the same high-frequency degradation, the features of these backbones exhibit only minor change. As such, we intend to build a representation trained for this task that serves as a texture-aware evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: A Backbone with a Texture Prior
sections.text: Texture discriminator. A representation for texture quality should be sensitive to the local statistics that distinguish real texture from generated texture. We construct supervision from real images to train the head: unmodified regions are positive, while synthetically perturbed regions serve as proxy negatives for contextually inconsistent texture alterations. The operators span three categories as discussed below: ( i ) Blur . The first category applies Gaussian, box, motion blur, and bicubic resampling. Natural defocus and motion blur follow scene depth and object motion and remain positive examples. Our negatives instead apply uniform blur within isolated semantic regions irrespective of depth, encouraging sensitivity to context-inconsistent over-smoothing rather than blur itself ( Wang et al. 2023 ; Kamali et al. 2025 ) . Thus, depth-consistent bokeh should remain compatible with the learned natural-image statistics. ( ii ) Spectral . The second category operates in the Fourier domain, reproducing alterations a blur cannot. Blur attenuates high frequencies smoothly and monotonically, while spectral operators selectively suppress a chosen band, targeting the band-specific spectral deviation of generated images ( Dzanic et al. 2020 ; Durall et al. 2020 ; Corvi et al. 2023 ) ; or alter phase while preserving magnitude, following the primacy of phase in perceptual structure ( Oppenheim and Lim 1981 ) . ( iii ) Noise . The third category adds Gaussian noise with constant variance. Sensor noise is a normal part of real imaging: its dominant photon-counting component is signal-dependent, scaling with local intensity ( Foi et al. 2008 ) . However, uniform, constant-variance Gaussian noise is a negative example of a sensor model. We apply this degradation to model the spurious fine detail some generators introduce as fake sharpness. We refer to details of these operators in Appendix. Regions and labels. For each image, we first partition it into regions using SAM2 ( Ravi et al. 2025 ) , where the output masks generally align with object and material boundaries and therefore separate regions of distinct texture. Each region is then either left unchanged or assigned a degradation operator from the pool. sections.text: With the learned backbone, we obtain the feature map 𝑭 ⁡ ( I ) {\bm{F}}(I) that provides a description of the texture at each location. When comparing the output of a generative model against real images, these statistics are of interest. In one dimension, this amounts to sorting the two sets of projections and comparing them in order. TRIG is this quantity, and a lower value indicates texture statistics closer to those of real images. The maximum mean discrepancy is a further nonparametric option, adopted by CMMD and by Gram-MMD. It requires a kernel bandwidth whose value affects the resulting score and is commonly set by heuristic ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) . We report SWD in the main experiments. sections.heading: Scores Across Generative Advances
sections.text: We compare various advanced generative models trained on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 ( Deng et al. 2009 ) , including diffusion models, flow-based models, autoregressive models, and GANs. We generate 50,000 images from each model. ImageNet-anchor is the real reference set against which every distance is computed, and ImageNet-eval provides a second real set, so that the distance between the two real sets shows the measured discrepancy on real data. Table. 1 reports the results. TRIG is shown with the SWD by default. Under every metric, the two real sets are the closest pair, and each generator receives a larger distance from the reference. More experimental details can be found in Appendix.

sections.heading: Agreement with Human Realism Rating
sections.text: In Table. 1 , we apply TRIG to various generative models. Whether these distances agree with human perception of texture realism is a separate question, on which we examine through two human studies in this section. We first adopt RAISE ( Mukherjee et al. 2025 ) , a dataset targets overall perceived realness rather than semantic contents. Each image carries a mean opinion score (MOS) from a human study, collected under instructions to judge realness independently of semantic content, making the dataset well-suited to a texture-oriented metric. Following the protocol of ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) , we order images by MOS into 24 groups and compute each distance against a fixed anchor of 1000 COCO images, reporting Spearman and Kendall τ \tau agreement against FID, KID, CMMD, and Gram-MMD (DINOv2 and DC-AE variants). sections.heading: 5 Ablation Study
sections.text: Table 4 reports the correlation with the RAISE benchmark and our ImageNet human study for several variants of TRIG. Pre-trained data. The backbone is a discriminator trained on textures, and we examine how pre-training data affect the performance. We observed that pretraining on textures consistently gives the strongest agreement with human judgment, whereas random initialization or pretraining on other datasets (e.g., FFHQ ( Karras et al. 2019 ) ), even directly on ImageNet, reduces performance. This therefore suggests the importance of our learned texture prior. Distribution distance. We next fix the representation and vary the distance used to compare image sets. The SWD and MMD produce comparable results, whereas the Fréchet distance (FD) performs worse. The similar behavior of the two nonparametric distances suggests that agreement with human judgment is determined primarily by the learned representation rather than by the particular distributional distance. Degradation. Finally, we examine the supervision used to train the plausibility head. Removing the noise degradations reduces agreement on RAISE and reverses the sign on ImageNet Study, indicating that noise provides an informative supervision. Removing blur also lowers agreement on both studies, while removing the frequency operators has a smaller effect; both contribute, but less critically than noise. Applying degradations without region masks likewise reduces agreement, suggesting that preserving object and material boundaries helps the representation learn realistic local texture. These results indicate that all degradation type and the spatial placement contribute to the learned representation. We refer to more ablation studies of design choices in Appendix. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented TRIG, a metric for evaluating generative models through texture realism. Instead of relying on representations trained for other vision tasks, TRIG learns a representation specifically for assessing the local texture. Compared to competing metrics, TRIG aligns more closely with human judgments of texture realism and can also produce spatial maps that localize inconsistent texture. As texture represents one aspect of image quality, we view TRIG as a complementary protocol to existing evaluation metrics.

sections.heading: Overview.
sections.text: This supplementary material provides additional details and results supporting the main paper. We first visualize the texture prior learned through GAN pretraining (Section A ). We then describe the full training protocol, including the degradation operators, the region-based degradation procedure, optimization settings, and dataset splits (Section B ). Then we discuss the implementation and computational properties of the three set-level distribution distances considered in the paper (Section C ). Section D reports additional ablations supporting our choice of fine-tuned layers and training hyperparameters. We then provide complete details of the ImageNet human study, covering study design, the ethics statement, preference aggregation, reliability analysis, bootstrap confidence intervals, and image sourcing and randomization (Section E ), and describe how we use the RAISE dataset and sample the COCO anchor set (Section F ). Finally, we probe TRIG further to check its sensitivity to texture quality perturbations (Section G ). We introduce more qualitative texture-realism maps responding to seen and unseen degradations across generators and image classes (Section H ).

sections.heading: Degradation Pool Details
sections.text: In this section, we provide the exact parameterization of the degradation pool 𝒫 \mathcal{P} used to train the plausibility head (summarized in Table 5 ). The pool contains seven operators across three categories, with nine strength variants in total. All severities are normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for the ordering loss.

sections.heading: Category 1: Blur (optical and resolution loss).
sections.text: In this category, we apply uniform or directional low-pass operators modeling AI-generated defocus, motion, and resolution loss. • Gaussian blur : convolution with an isotropic Gaussian kernel, applied at two strength ranges, σ ∈ [ 3 , 8 ] \sigma\in[3,8] (light) and σ ∈ [ 8 , 15 ] \sigma\in[8,15] (heavy); severity = σ / 15 =\sigma/15 . • Box blur : uniform k × k k\times k averaging kernel, k ∈ { 7 , 11 , 15 } k\in\{7,11,15\} ; severity = k / 15 =k/15 . • Motion blur : 1 × L 1\times L horizontal averaging kernel (linear motion), L ∈ [ 10 , 25 ] L\in[10,25] ; severity = L / 25 =L/25 . • Bicubic resample : bicubic downsampling to resolution R / s R/s followed by upsampling back to R R , with s ∈ [ 2 , 4 ] s\in[2,4] (i.e. → { 128 ​ … ​ 64 } → 256 256\!\to\!\{128\dots 64\}\!\to\!256 ); severity = ( s − 1 ) / 3 =(s-1)/3 .

sections.heading: Natural defocus versus artificial over-smoothing.
sections.text: We stress that blur is not intrinsically unrealistic. Natural shallow depth of field follows lens optics and scene depth, producing defocus patterns and focus transitions that remain consistent with scene geometry. Such patterns are retained in the undegraded real photographs used as positive samples. In contrast, our proxy degradation applies a single blur kernel uniformly within a selected region, without access to depth, optical parameters, or motion, thereby introducing contextually inconsistent loss of detail. The multiscale feature pyramid can evaluate this local frequency change together with its surrounding structure, rather than responding to low-frequency content alone. sections.heading: Degradation Application Protocol
sections.text: Degradations are applied per region: each image is partitioned using SAM2. If SAM2 returns fewer than three valid regions, we instead use an N×N regular grid, with N ∈ [ 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 ] N\in[4,8,16,32,64] . For each image, we sample the clean-region probability p c ​ l ​ e ​ a ​ n ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.3 , 0.7 ) p_{clean}\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}(0.3,0.7) , after which each region is independently left unchanged with probability p c ​ l ​ e ​ a ​ n p_{clean} . Otherwise, one of the seven degradation operators is sampled uniformly and applied at a randomly sampled strength. Unchanged regions receive label 1, and synthetically perturbed regions receive label 0. Severity is not used as a regression target, since strengths are not comparable across operator types; instead, the ranking loss (Eq.6 in main paper) enforces monotonicity within an operator type, requiring that for two same-type regions with | Δ ​ severity | ≥ δ |\Delta\text{severity}|\geq\delta the more degraded region scores lower. The Gaussian-blur and noise operators each include two strength ranges to guarantee that same-type pairs exist for the ranking loss.

sections.heading: Role of synthetic degradations.
sections.text: We emphasize that the degradation operators used for fine-tuning are proxy perturbations rather than an exhaustive definition of unrealistic texture. Blur and noise may occur naturally in real photographs, and their presence alone does not imply poor texture realism. Our operators instead expose the backbone to controlled attenuation, alteration, or amplification of local texture statistics resembling artifacts observed in generated images. Accordingly, the binary labels indicate whether a synthetic perturbation was applied, rather than whether the resulting region must be universally perceptually inconsistent. We show some examples of our training data by overlaying SAM2 mask on real image and apply various degradation to one selected region, as shown in Figure 11 . The transfer from these proxy perturbations to generated-image texture realism is evaluated independently through the two human studies reported in the main paper. sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: The backbone comprises StyleGAN3 discriminator blocks { b256 , b128 , b64 , b32 , b16 } \{\mathrm{b256,b128,b64,b32,b16}\} . For a 256 × 256 256\times 256 input, the FPN receives features from b16 \mathrm{b16} , b32 \mathrm{b32} , b64 \mathrm{b64} , and b128 \mathrm{b128} with shapes 512 × 8 × 8 512\times 8\times 8 , 512 × 16 × 16 512\times 16\times 16 , 512 × 32 × 32 512\times 32\times 32 , and 512 × 64 × 64 512\times 64\times 64 , respectively. Each is projected to 128 channels by a 1 × 1 1\times 1 lateral convolution. Beginning at 8 × 8 8\times 8 , each top-down stage bilinearly upsamples the coarser map by 2, adds the corresponding lateral map, and applies a 3 × 3 3\times 3 , 128-channel convolution followed by LeakyReLU with slope 0.2. A 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution from 128 to 64 channels, LeakyReLU, and a 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution from 64 to 1 channel produce the 1 × 64 × 64 1\times 64\times 64 logit map. Global average pooling of the final 128-channel FPN map gives the 128-dimensional image descriptor, while the single-image texture-consistency score is the spatial mean of the sigmoid output map.

sections.heading: Frozen and trainable components.
sections.text: Discriminator blocks b256 \mathrm{b256} – b16 \mathrm{b16} are frozen, while the FPN and texture-realism head, containing 747,009 parameters, are trainable. Blocks b8 \mathrm{b8} and b4 \mathrm{b4} remain frozen and are not used in the FPN forward pass.

sections.heading: Preprocessing.
sections.text: Images are converted to RGB, resized directly to 256 × 256 256\times 256 without preserving aspect ratio using Lanczos interpolation, converted to floating-point tensors, and mapped channel-wise from [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . We use no cropping, five-crop evaluation, flipping, or color augmentation. SAM2 region masks are precomputed, with regular grids used as a fallback.

sections.heading: Optimization and objective.
sections.text: We use AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , batch size 8, and global gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. Cosine annealing is applied over 50,000 steps and ends at 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , or 1% of the initial learning rate. The objective is ℒ = ℒ BCE + λ ​ ℒ ord , λ = 0.5 . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ord}},\qquad\lambda=0.5. Clean map cells are labeled 1 and degraded cells 0. For region pairs receiving the same degradation type and differing in normalized severity by at least δ = 0.1 \delta=0.1 , we use ℒ ord = max ⁡ ( 0 , p severe − p mild + η ) , η = 0.05 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ord}}=\max(0,p_{\mathrm{severe}}-p_{\mathrm{mild}}+\eta),\qquad\eta=0.05.

sections.heading: Perceptual Judgments: 2AFC
sections.text: Unlike some classification tasks which can be supervised by clear ground truth, the perceived realism depends more on subjective preference. To fill this gap, there is a long-standing paradigm from psychophysics for quantifying perception. The two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) protocol, dating back to Fechner’s foundational work in 1860s ( Fechner 1860 ) , presents an observer with two stimuli and asks which exhibits a given perceptual attribute more strongly. Because a relative pairwise judgment avoids the calibration and scale-drift problems of absolute rating scales, 2AFC has become a workhorse for subjective image-and video-quality assessment, valued for its high discrimination power and reliability ( Ding et al. 2021 ; Prashnani et al. 2018 ) . Another consideration in forced-choice studies is whether to permit an “undecided”/tie response: allowing ties yields more faithful data when stimuli are genuinely indistinguishable, at the cost of discarding those trials from the decisive signal ( Men et al. 2023 ) . We therefore adopted a 2AFC-style pairwise comparison augmented with a tie option to obtain a ground-truth ordering of image sources by perceived texture realism , and the procedure for correlating each distribution metric against it.

Each trial draws one ImageNet class, two distinct sources, and one random image from each source within that class; the two images are randomly assigned to the left/right panes. Every session uses a fresh random seed, so no two participants see the same trial sequence. All relevant images and human judgments will be released together with our source code. sections.text: Participants judge which image has more realistic surface texture , such as fur, skin, foliage, fabric, grain, rather than which image is sharper. When both sides appear equally real or equally fake, participants select Tie . Sources are hidden and the interface is fully blind.

sections.heading: Ethics statement.
sections.text: This work includes a human perceptual study to evaluate the realism of generated images. Participants were informed about the purpose of the study and voluntarily provided their judgments. No personally identifiable information or sensitive personal data were collected, and responses were analyzed only in aggregate. Participants were free to stop the study at any time. All participants have normal or corrected to normal vision. No payments are provided. The images used in the study were generated by publicly available generative models or obtained from publicly available datasets, and the study involved only perceptual comparisons without exposing participants to sensitive or harmful content. We believe the risks associated with this study are minimal.

sections.heading: Aggregating Pairwise Judgments
sections.text: We collected 24 completed sessions, and no participant was excluded. We convert the 4,800 pairwise judgments into a per-source realness score in two ways, which agree strongly (Spearman + 0.983 +0.983 over the eight generators). Correlations are computed over n=9 non-anchor sources: eight generators and one real set. We only use one of real sets because the two real sets are theoretically identical, and they only serve as a sanity check.

sections.heading: Win-rate (primary).
sections.text: For each source, win-rate = ( wins + 0.5 ⋅ ties ) / games \text{win-rate}=(\text{wins}+0.5\cdot\text{ties})/\text{games} , counted over all opponents. Higher values indicate greater perceived realism. Figure 13: Human preference ranking. Per-source win-rate for all ten sources, sorted, with 95 % 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The two real sets (green) sit well above the chance line ( 0.5 0.5 ); the eight generators cluster at or below chance with overlapping intervals, showing that generator-vs-generator preference is weaker while real-vs-generated is decisive.

sections.heading: Bradley–Terry.
sections.text: We also fit a Bradley–Terry ( Hunter 2004 ) model by the Hunter MM maximum likelihood estimator, yielding mean-centered log-strengths β \beta (higher = = more real). Both scores place the two real sets clearly at the top and the generators near or below the 0.5 0.5 chance line, consistent with humans reliably distinguishing real from generated while struggling to separate one generator from another. We report the resulting human ranking with trial-level bootstrap confidence intervals in Figure 13 .

sections.heading: Split-half reliability.
sections.text: We assessed the reliability of the source ranking using 2,000 random participant-level splits with a fixed seed. In each repetition, the 24 participants were divided into two disjoint groups of 12, source win rates were recomputed independently in each half, and the resulting rankings were compared using Spearman’s rank correlation. For the nine sources included in the primary ranking analysis, the median split-half correlation was ρ = 0.917 \rho=0.917 , with a central 95% range of [ 0.767 , 0.983 ] [0.767,\,0.983] across random splits. Applying the Spearman–Brown correction yielded an estimated full-study reliability of 0.957 0.957 , with a central 95% range of [ 0.868 , 0.992 ] [0.868,\,0.992] . Reliability remained high when considering all ten sources ( 0.969 0.969 corrected) or only the eight generated-image sources ( 0.937 0.937 corrected), indicating that the source ordering is stable across independent subsets of participants.

sections.text: We quantify uncertainty in the metric–human correlations using two non-parametric bootstrap procedures. Our primary analysis uses a trial-level bootstrap that samples 4,800 individual trials with replacement, and we also report a participant-level cluster bootstrap that samples the 24 participants with replacement while retaining all trials from each selected participant. The residual semantic component thus helps a semantic metric like CMMD on the ambiguous ranking task, but it is absent on RAISE’s per-image ratings, where CMMD fails. sections.heading: Appendix G Does the metric respond to semantics or texture?
sections.text: We probe what each metric responds to by adding Gaussian blur of increasing strength to all sources (full 50k). Blur preserves semantic content while progressively destroying texture detail, so a texture-oriented metric should react strongly to it, whereas a semantics-oriented metric should be comparatively insensitive. Figure 17 shows each metric’s score for the real ImageNet-eval set and 12 generators as blur strength increases; the metrics respond in markedly different ways. FID and KID, built on an Inception classifier that encodes “what is in the image,” are nearly invariant to mild blur and then respond in the wrong direction: under heavy blur they rate the real ImageNet set as less realistic than the generated sets, revealing that their features track semantic content rather than texture. CMMD and Gram-MMD continue to separate the sources even under strong blur; since blur has by then removed most texture information, this residual separability indicates that they too rank largely by semantic or global structure rather than texture. TRIG behaves oppositely: as blur destroys texture detail, the scores of all sources converge, suggesting its sensitivity to texture realism. This convergence is the expected behavior of a metric driven by texture quality, providing evidence that TRIG is particularly sensitive to texture degradation rather than relying primarily on semantic content. Figure 17: Metric score vs. blur strength for the real ImageNet set and 12 generators. As blur becomes severe, FID and KID rate the generated sets as more realistic than the real set (wrong direction); CMMD and Gram-MMD (DINOv2) keep separating the sources even when texture is largely destroyed; TRIG’s scores converge as texture detail is removed, consistent with a metric driven by texture quality.

sections.text: Beyond the generated images evaluated in the main paper, we probe how the texture-realism map of our backbone responds to controlled, manually applied degradations. sections.heading: Per-operator response.
sections.text: We first apply each of the seven degradation operators to the full image. In every case the heatmap turns red over the degraded texture while the background remains green, confirming that TRIG responds to each operator type rather than to a single artifact. The original (undegraded) image yields a nearly uniform green map, and the response is strongest for the operators that most disrupt local texture statistics (Gaussian, box, and motion blur), consistent with the training supervision.

sections.heading: Response to degradation coverage.
sections.text: Then we apply blurred blocks at increasing coverage ( n = 5 n=5 to n = 80 n=80 blocks). The red response grows monotonically with coverage, indicating that the map reflects the extent of degraded texture rather than merely flagging its presence.

Jiali Cui Zhiqiang Lao Heather Yu Liang Peng † † thanks: Corresponding author. Abstract This paper studies the backbone used by metrics for evaluating the quality of generated images. Although generative models have advanced rapidly, some outputs still exhibit unrealistic texture characteristics, and these differences are difficult to measure. Widely used evaluation metrics provide limited insight into texture realism, since they often rely on a backbone trained for another objective, such as image classification or image-text alignment. Such objectives typically encourage invariance to low-level variations that carry texture, so the resulting features primarily encode semantic and global structure. As a result, texture-specific discrepancies may not be explicitly captured. We propose TRIG, a metric directed at the texture realism of generated images. Its backbone is instead the discriminator of a generative adversarial network pre-trained on a texture dataset, which provides a learned prior for the local statistics of natural textures. A plausibility head is fine-tuned to identify local texture degradations, while preserving natural defocus and sensor noise as positive cases. On the features of this backbone, we compute a standard distributional distance between a reference set of real images and a set of generated ones. We apply TRIG to several generative models and observe closer agreement with human realness ratings than baseline metrics. 1 Northwestern University 2 Futurewei Technologies 1 Introduction Progress in image generation quality is largely measured by automated metrics. The standard approach compares a set of generated images with a set of real ones in the feature space of a pretrained network, and reports a distance between the two distributions. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al. 2017 ) and the Kernel Inception Distance (KID) ( Bińkowski et al. 2018 ) follow this pattern with features from an image classifier, and CLIP Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) ( Jayasumana et al. 2024 ) follows it with embeddings trained for image-text alignment. A separate line of work ( Sajjadi et al. 2018 ; Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ) reports precision and recall in place of a single distance, in order to distinguish the fidelity of generated samples from their diversity. Although these methods differ in Real DiT ADM StyleGAN-XL Original Images Fourier Spectra Figure 1: Real and generated images with their Fourier spectra. Compared with natural photographs, generated images exhibit characteristic spectral artifacts, particularly in the mid-to-high frequency range, despite appearing visually similar in the image domain. how they compare distributions, they primarily rely on representations learned for particular objectives, and thus influence which discrepancies between real and generated images the resulting metrics are sensitive to. Modern generative models now reproduce scene content and global structure remarkably well, while often differing from photographs in the statistics of local texture. These differences contribute to a perceived lack of realism even when observers cannot point to their source, and they become more evident in the frequency domain (Figure 1 ). Recent work ( Stein et al. 2023 ) has shown that the choice of representation is a major source of disagreement between automated metrics and human judgment, motivating alternatives based on self-supervised representations ( Caron et al. 2021 ; Oquab et al. 2024 ) rather than image classification. Although these representations capture richer visual information, they remain optimized for objectives that encourage invariance to low-level appearance changes, including much of the variation that characterizes texture (see discussion in Section. 3 ). Recent texture-oriented metrics ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) likewise extract statistics from such backbones, which can be limited for assessing texture realism itself. Texture realism, however, is not equivalent to sharpness. Real photographs naturally contain blur, sensor noise, and other imperfections arising from the image formation process: backgrounds fall outside the depth of field ( Levoy and Hanrahan 1996 ) , moving objects produce motion blur ( Levin et al. 2008 ) , and photon-limited imaging introduces visible noise under low illumination ( Foi et al. 2008 ) . Therefore, measuring whether the local texture is consistent with statistics derived from physical image formation remains challenging. Motivated by this perspective, we learn a representation specifically for texture realism instead of adapting one trained for another task. We begin with the discriminator of a generative adversarial network (GANs) ( Goodfellow et al. 2014 ; Liu et al. 2019 ; Lin et al. 2023 ) trained on textures, whose objective is to distinguish real textures from synthesized ones. The early layers are kept frozen to preserve this learned texture prior, while a lightweight prediction head is trained to produce dense spatial features. Training such prediction head uses only real photographs, where synthetic degradations are adaptively applied. The degradations are chosen to produce texture statistics that are unlikely to arise through physical image formation. As such, the resulting representation produces, at each spatial location, a score reflecting consistency with learned natural-texture statistics. For evaluating generative models, these features are pooled within each image and compared across image sets using a distributional distance. We refer to the resulting metric as TRIG. We evaluate TRIG on various generative models and compare it with widely used automatic metrics. We also examine our metric for agreement with two human studies, where in both settings, TRIG exhibits closer agreement with human judgments than the competing metrics. We further analyze the spatial responses of the learned representation, showing that both the image-level score and the texture-realism map identify regions whose texture can differ from that of real photographs. Finally, ablation studies examine the contribution of each component of the proposed method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce TRIG , a distributional metric that evaluates generative models through a representation learned specifically for texture realism. • We propose a spatially supervised texture representation by adapting a texture GAN discriminator and fine-tuning it with localized synthetic degradations. • We apply TRIG to various generative models and find that TRIG better agrees with human judgments of texture realism than widely used metrics, while providing spatial maps that localize inconsistent texture. 2 Related Works Metrics for image generation. Most evaluation metrics compare generated and real images in the feature space of a pretrained network. The Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al. 2016 ) summarizes the predictions of an image classifier, while FID ( Heusel et al. 2017 ) and KID ( Bińkowski et al. 2018 ) compare feature distributions extracted by the same backbone using Fréchet and kernel distances, respectively. CMMD replaces the classification features with representations from a vision-language model. Complementary metrics report precision and recall, or density and coverage, to separately characterize sample fidelity and diversity ( Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ; Naeem et al. 2020 ) . Several studies examine the reliability of these metrics, and most target the Inception representation they rely on rather than the comparison itself. Parmar et al. (2022) show that low-level operations such as aliased resizing and compression alter the extracted features and thus the reported score, and propose corrected preprocessing. Chong and Forsyth (2020) show that the FID estimator is biased in a way that depends on the model being evaluated, and derive a debiased variant. CMMD ( Jayasumana et al. 2024 ) instead changes both components: it replaces Inception with CLIP features and the Fréchet distance with the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). These works patch the backbone, debias the estimator, or substitute a different generic backbone, but none learn a representation tailored to texture; this is the gap our method addresses. The choice of feature extractor. Recent work argues that the representation largely determines agreement with human perception. ( Stein et al. 2023 ) show that classification features correlate poorly with human judgments and recommend replacing them with self-supervised feature extractors, such as DINOv2-ViT-L/14 ( Oquab et al. 2024 ) . Gram-MMD ( Napolitano and Nguyen 2026 ) instead targets texture by computing Gram statistics from intermediate features of a pretrained backbone selected through a search over layers. Despite these differences, all of these methods rely on representations learned for object recognition other than texture assessment. We instead train a representation specifically for texture realism by adapting a texture discriminator and fine-tuning it with supervision designed for this task. From texture representation to image quality assessment. The statistical description of texture has a long history in image processing, originally developed for texture synthesis. ( Portilla and Simoncelli 2000 ) represent a texture by a compact set of multiscale wavelet statistics and re-synthesize textures that match them. ( Gatys et al. 2015 ) and ( Heitz et al. 2021 ) instead extract features from a pretrained VGG ( Simonyan and Zisserman 2015 ) network, matching either their Gram matrices or, in the case of ( Heitz et al. 2021 ) , their full feature distributions via a sliced Wasserstein distance. In all cases the goal is to find a representation in which two textures that look alike are close, and to synthesize a texture that matches a target under that representation. This suggests a natural extension to evaluation: if similar textures yield similar representations, then the distance between representations can measure texture similarity. Gram-MMD follows this idea by computing MMD over Gram statistics extracted from selected layers of a pretrained backbone. We adopt the same premise, but argue that the representation should be learned for texture realism instead of a second-order statistic of features from a backbone trained for an unrelated semantic task. 3 Methods Texture Quality in Real Imaging We study the problem of assessing the texture quality of images produced by generative models. By texture quality , we mean the consistency between local texture statistics in images and those in real images. A real image may contain a defocused background, motion blur from a moving subject, or sensor noise in a dimly lit region. These effects can arise naturally during image formation and therefore do not by themselves indicate unrealistic texture. Generated images may instead exhibit local texture discrepancies that are not explained by these natural effects, such as spatially inconsistent loss of high-frequency detail (see Figure. 1 for examples with their Fourier spectra). The question we ask of an image is therefore not how sharp it is, but whether its texture is consistent with the surrounding visual context. As such, we intend to build a representation trained for this task that serves as a texture-aware evaluation protocol. A Backbone with a Texture Prior Texture discriminator. A representation for texture quality should be sensitive to the local statistics that distinguish real texture from generated texture. In this work, we consider the discriminator of a generative adversarial network (GANs), which is trained on the real texture dataset ( Lin et al. 2024 ) and optimized to separate real texture from synthesized texture. As texture images contain little semantic content (see Figure. 3 for examples), such a discriminator primarily captures local statistics instead of object semantics, and learned features encode the regularities of real textures, providing a learned prior for assessing texture quality. We construct supervision from real images to train the head: unmodified regions are positive, while synthetically perturbed regions serve as proxy negatives for contextually inconsistent texture alterations. The operators span three categories as discussed below: ( i ) Blur . The first category applies Gaussian, box, motion blur, and bicubic resampling. Natural defocus and motion blur follow scene depth and object motion and remain positive examples. Our negatives instead apply uniform blur within isolated semantic regions irrespective of depth, encouraging sensitivity to context-inconsistent over-smoothing rather than blur itself ( Wang et al. 2023 ; Kamali et al. 2025 ) . Thus, depth-consistent bokeh should remain compatible with the learned natural-image statistics. ( ii ) Spectral . The second category operates in the Fourier domain, reproducing alterations a blur cannot. Blur attenuates high frequencies smoothly and monotonically, while spectral operators selectively suppress a chosen band, targeting the band-specific spectral deviation of generated images ( Dzanic et al. 2020 ; Durall et al. 2020 ; Corvi et al. 2023 ) ; or alter phase while preserving magnitude, following the primacy of phase in perceptual structure ( Oppenheim and Lim 1981 ) . ( iii ) Noise . The third category adds Gaussian noise with constant variance. Sensor noise is a normal part of real imaging: its dominant photon-counting component is signal-dependent, scaling with local intensity ( Foi et al. 2008 ) . However, uniform, constant-variance Gaussian noise is a negative example of a sensor model. We apply this degradation to model the spurious fine detail some generators introduce as fake sharpness. We refer to details of these operators in Appendix. Regions and labels. For each image, we first partition it into regions using SAM2 ( Ravi et al. 2025 ) , where the output masks generally align with object and material boundaries and therefore separate regions of distinct texture. Each region is then either left unchanged or assigned a degradation operator from the pool. Pre-trained data. The backbone is a discriminator trained on textures, and we examine how pre-training data affect the performance. We observed that pretraining on textures consistently gives the strongest agreement with human judgment, whereas random initialization or pretraining on other datasets (e.g., FFHQ ( Karras et al. 2019 ) ), even directly on ImageNet, reduces performance. This therefore suggests the importance of our learned texture prior. Distribution distance. We next fix the representation and vary the distance used to compare image sets. The SWD and MMD produce comparable results, whereas the Fréchet distance (FD) performs worse. The similar behavior of the two nonparametric distances suggests that agreement with human judgment is determined primarily by the learned representation rather than by the particular distributional distance. Degradation. Finally, we examine the supervision used to train the plausibility head. Removing the noise degradations reduces agreement on RAISE and reverses the sign on ImageNet Study, indicating that noise provides an informative supervision. Removing blur also lowers agreement on both studies, while removing the frequency operators has a smaller effect; both contribute, but less critically than noise. Applying degradations without region masks likewise reduces agreement, suggesting that preserving object and material boundaries helps the representation learn realistic local texture. These results indicate that all degradation type and the spatial placement contribute to the learned representation. We refer to more ablation studies of design choices in Appendix.
